title: Pick out the finite subcover

prereqs.why: A finite subcover is what compactness promises, and here it has to be produced explicitly.
The space is closed and bounded in the line, which is why a finite subcover is guaranteed to exist at all.
The set is the standard example of a convergent sequence together with its limit, which is what makes it compact.

statement:
Let

$$K = \{0\} \cup \Bigl\{\tfrac1n : n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\Bigr\} \subset \R$$

with the usual metric. $K$ is closed and bounded, so by Heine–Borel it is
compact: **every** open cover of it has a finite subcover.

Consider the cover $\mathcal{U} = \{U_0, U_1, U_2, U_3, \dots\}$ given by

$$U_0 = \Bigl(-\tfrac{1}{10},\ \tfrac{1}{10}\Bigr), \qquad
U_n = \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\,n + \tfrac12\,},\ \tfrac{1}{\,n - \tfrac12\,}\Bigr)
\ \text{ for } n \ge 1.$$

Each $U_n$ with $n \ge 1$ contains exactly one point of $K$, namely $1/n$.

There is a unique **smallest** finite subcover. Give the set of its indices.

Write it like `{0,1,2}`.
hints: $U_0$ is the only member that contains $0$, so index 0 is in every subcover.
Which points $1/n$ does $U_0$ already cover? The condition is $1/n < 1/10$.
Be careful at the boundary: $U_0$ is open, so $1/10$ itself is **not** in it. Does that mean index 10 is needed, or not?
Every point of $K$ that $U_0$ misses needs its own $U_n$, because no other member of the cover contains it. Count how many that is.

payload.prompt: The indices of the smallest finite subcover.
payload.label: Indices
